☐ Prescription list (people + dog) ☐ Birth certificates / SS cards / passports
☐ Hotel confirmations (all nights) ☐ Cash ($200+ in small bills) + backup credit card

**🐕 DOG BAG**
☐ Food (trip + 1 week, same brand) ☐ Gallon of water from home ☐ Collapsible bowl
☐ Meds + calming / anti-nausea meds from vet ☐ Leash + backup leash + long lead
☐ Collar with tag (cell #) + GPS tracker ☐ Poop bags ☐ Crate or crash-tested harness
☐ Bed / blanket that smells like home ☐ Favorite toy + chew ☐ Towels + enzymatic cleaner
☐ Pet first-aid kit ☐ Recent photo of dog (in case lost)

**🚗 CAR KIT**
☐ Phone chargers + power bank ☐ Offline maps downloaded ☐ Sunshades
☐ Jumper cables / jump pack ☐ Tire gauge ☐ Flashlight ☐ First-aid kit
☐ Paper towels, wipes, trash bags ☐ Cooler with snacks + water ☐ Roadside assistance #

**🧳 OVERNIGHT BAGS (4 nights each)**
☐ Clothes ☐ Toiletries ☐ Personal meds ☐ Laptops + work gear
☐ Valuables (jewelry, hard drives, irreplaceables)

**📦 OPEN-FIRST BOX (rides in car)**
☐ Toilet paper ☐ Sheets + pillows ☐ Towels ☐ Box cutter ☐ Basic tools + tape
☐ Light bulbs ☐ Paper plates + utensils ☐ Coffee setup ☐ Soap + dish soap ☐ Shower curtain

**✅ BEFORE YOU DRIVE AWAY**
☐ Every room, closet, cabinet empty ☐ Photo/video walk-through ☐ Meter photos
☐ Bill of Lading reviewed and signed (no blank forms) ☐ Thermostat set, windows locked
☐ Keys, remotes, and fobs returned (get receipt) ☐ Dog is in the car, not loose in the house

**📞 KEY CONTACTS**
Mover: __________ Car shipper: __________ Landlord (new): __________

## 💰 BUDGET TABLE (Completed)

**Remaining line items**

| Item | Estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Car trailer / tow dolly (DIY truck option) | $300–$700 | Tows car #2 behind the truck |
| Storage-in-transit (if mover delivery is late) | $150–$500/mo | Interstate movers often quote a 7–21 day delivery window |
| Contingency fund | 10–15% of total | Recommended. Something always comes up |

**Scenario totals** *(excludes rent, security deposits, and temporary housing, since those depend on your new place)*

| Scenario | Ballpark Total | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| **A. DIY truck** + tow car #2 + drive car #1 with dog | **$3,750–$9,000** | Lowest cost, but you do all the labor, and towing through the Rockies is tiring |
| **B. Portable container** + drive car #1 + ship car #2 | **$4,900–$9,900** | Middle ground: you pack and load, they drive |
| **C. Full-service movers** + drive car #1 + ship car #2 | **$7,500–$15,000+** | Least stress, highest cost |

**Add-ons:** temporary housing ($800–$2,000), first month's rent + deposit, and 10–15% contingency.

**Vehicle comparison**

| Option | Ballpark | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Drive one + ship one** | **$1,700–$2,850** | Dog rides with you. You both share driving. You have a car on arrival. Documents stay with you. | Shipping costs. Car #2 may arrive days after you. |
| **Drive both** | **$1,050–$1,800** | Cheapest. Both cars arrive with you. | Two solo drivers for ~2,400 miles. No driving relief. Wear on both cars. |
| **Ship both + fly** | **$2,500–$5,500+** | Fastest trip | Rental car until cars arrive (7–14 days). Flying the dog is the big problem (see below). |

**Why flying is hard for your dog in July:**
- **Small dog** (under ~20 lbs with carrier): in-cabin fee of about $125–$200. This is manageable.
- **Larger dog:** cargo or pet transport costs $500–$4,000. Many airlines restrict cargo pets in summer heat, and snub-nosed breeds are often banned entirely.

**Recommendation:** Drive one car with the dog and ship the other. It's the best balance of cost, safety, and sanity for a July move.

## 📦 ROOM-BY-ROOM PACKING (continued)

**Week 3–2: Living Room / Office** *(continued)*
☐ Take furniture apart. Put hardware in labeled zip bags taped to the underside of the matching piece, or keep all hardware bags in one "Hardware" box that rides in the car.
☐ TVs in TV boxes or wrapped in moving blankets. Never lay a flat-screen flat.

☐ **M** Back up both computers and phones to cloud + external drive. Carry the external drive in the car.
☐ **P** Pack work equipment last (or carry it) if either of you works remotely during the move

**Week 2–1: Kitchen**
☐ Pack rarely used items first: specialty appliances, serving dishes, extra glassware, bakeware
☐ Dishes stacked **vertically** like records, with paper between each. Use dish-pack boxes.
☐ Glasses and stemware in cell-divider boxes
☐ Knives wrapped in towels or cardboard, labeled "SHARP"
☐ Use up pantry and freezer food starting week 3. Donate unopened food to a food bank.
☐ Toss opened liquids (oil, vinegar, sauces). They leak, and movers won't take perishables.
☐ Keep out a "last week kit": 1 pot, 1 pan, 2 plates/bowls/mugs, utensils, dish soap, sponge, coffee setup
☐ Small appliances (blender, toaster) cleaned and dry, with cords taped to them
☐ Fridge: empty, clean, and unplug 24 hrs before. Leave doors propped open.

**Week 1: Bedrooms**
☐ Wardrobe boxes for hanging clothes (move straight from closet to box)
☐ Dresser drawers: lightweight clothes can stay inside if the mover allows. Remove anything heavy or breakable.
☐ Mattresses in mattress bags (about $10–$20 each). This keeps them clean and dry.
☐ Bed frames taken apart, with hardware bagged and labeled
☐ Jewelry and valuables go in the car, never on the truck
☐ Pack each person's suitcase for 4–5 nights of road travel, plus 1 week of arrival clothes

**Week 1 (Final Days): Bathrooms**
☐ Toss expired meds and nearly empty products
☐ Tighten caps, and put plastic wrap under lids for liquids. Bag everything in zip bags.
☐ Prescriptions and daily meds go in the car
☐ Pack an "open first" bathroom kit: toilet paper, shower curtain + rings, towels, soap, shampoo, toothbrushes, hand towel, plunger
☐ Cleaning supplies: keep one kit out for the move-out clean, then toss or give away flammable ones

## 📁 PAPERWORK: WHAT TRAVELS WHERE

**Carry in the car (document pouch, never on the truck)**
- IDs, passports, birth certificates, Social Security cards
- Vehicle titles, registrations, insurance cards
- Both leases / closing docs

**Scan to the cloud (shared folder both of you can access)**

**OK to ship (sealed and labeled)**

## ✂️ DECLUTTER TIPS

1. **The weight rule:** Interstate moves are priced largely by weight. If an item costs less to rebuy in Oregon than to ship, sell it. Cheap particleboard furniture, old mattresses, and bulky low-value items are prime candidates.
2. **The 12-month rule:** If you haven't used it in a year and it's not sentimental, let it go.
3. **Measure the new place first.** Don't move a couch that won't fit through the door or a dining table that's too big for the room.
4. **Sell big items early (weeks 8–5).** Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist sales slow down when you're desperate. List furniture you'll live without first.
5. **Book donation pickups 2–3 weeks ahead.** Habitat for Humanity ReStore, Salvation Army, and local charities pick up furniture, but their schedules fill fast.
6. **Use one room as a staging zone** with marked areas for "Sell," "Donate," "Trash," and "Keep." Clear it weekly.
7. **Do 30–60 minutes a day** rather than marathon weekends. Each of you takes certain rooms.
8. **Sentimental items:** Photograph anything you're letting go of but want to remember.
9. **Eat down the pantry.** Plan meals around what's in the freezer starting 3 weeks out.
10. **Oregon-specific:** Ohio winters need heavy snow gear. Western Oregon needs rain gear. Keep a light winter kit if you plan to go to the mountains, and sell the rest.

## 🐕 DOG TRAVEL CHECKLIST

**⚠️ Correction to Part 1:** I said a health certificate (CVI) was only needed if flying. Oregon's animal import rules generally **do** require dogs entering the state to have a CVI issued within 30 days and a current rabies vaccine, even by car. Enforcement on car travel is rare, but it's inexpensive ($50–$150) and hotels or emergency vets may ask for records. Confirm with the Oregon Department of Agriculture, then **book the vet visit for July 1–10** so it's within the 30-day window.

**Before the Trip (Weeks 8–2)**
☐ **M** Vet visit: health check, rabies and vaccines current, CVI (timed as above), refill meds, ask about anti-nausea (e.g., Cerenia) or anti-anxiety meds. **Do a trial dose at home** before travel day.
☐ **M** Confirm microchip is registered and working (vet can scan it). Update the phone number now and the address after you arrive.
☐ **M** New ID tag with your **cell numbers** (not the Ohio landline or address)
☐ **M** Get a GPS tracker (AirTag-style collar holder or a dedicated pet GPS) for the road
☐ **J** Crash-tested harness or a secured crate. The dog rides in the back seat or cargo area, never the front seat (airbags).
☐ **J** Practice runs: 2–3 drives of 1–2 hours in the setup you'll use
☐ **M** Buy enough of the **same food** for the trip + 2 weeks. Switching food during a move upsets stomachs.

**Route Planning**
- **Likely route:** I-70 or I-80 west through Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah, then I-84 through Idaho into Oregon. Roughly 2,300–2,500 miles depending on your exact start and end.
- **Recommended pace with a dog:** 4–5 days, 450–600 miles/day
- **Sample 5-day split:**
  - Day 1: Ohio → eastern Iowa (Iowa City / Des Moines)
  - Day 2: → central Nebraska (Kearney / North Platte)
  - Day 3: → southwest Wyoming (Rock Springs / Evanston)
  - Day 4: → Boise area
  - Day 5: → Oregon destination
☐ **M** Mark a **24-hour emergency vet** near each overnight stop and save the numbers
☐ **M** Pull up dog-friendly rest areas or parks every 2–3 hours
☐ **J** Check wildfire smoke (AirNow.gov) and heat forecasts the week of departure. July can bring smoke in Idaho and Oregon and 95°F+ heat in the plains.

**Lodging**
☐ **M** Book every night ahead with written pet-policy confirmation (weight limit, number of pets, fee). Many chains are dog-friendly, but rules vary **by location**, so confirm with each specific hotel.
☐ Expect $25–$75/night pet fees
☐ Ask for a ground-floor room near an exit for easy potty trips
☐ **Don't leave the dog alone in a hotel room** unless the hotel allows it. A stressed dog in a strange room may bark or chew.

**Car Comfort**
☐ AC on and working well. Check the back seat gets enough airflow.
☐ Window sunshades for the back seats
☐ Seat cover or hammock, plus the home blanket or bed
☐ Water every stop (spill-proof bowl in the car)
☐ Light meal in the morning 2–3 hrs before driving and the main meal at night to reduce car sickness
☐ Long walk before loading each morning
☐ **Never leave the dog in a parked car in July, not even for 5 minutes.** Interior temperatures can reach deadly levels in minutes. Use drive-thrus, eat at patio restaurants, or take turns going inside so one person stays with the dog and the AC running.

**Overnight Routine**
☐ Walk the dog first, then bring in bags
☐ Set up the crate or bed, bowls, and toy in the same arrangement each night
☐ Keep the leash on in parking lots and near doors. Dogs in new places bolt.
☐ Feed dinner, then a calm evening walk
☐ Keep a portable "hotel bag" separate (food for 1 night, bowls, poop bags, meds, towel) so you're not unpacking the whole car

**Moving Day (Ohio)**
☐ Board the dog or have a friend keep them during loading, **or** crate them in an empty room with a "DO NOT OPEN" sign on the door
☐ Dog bag packed and in the car **before** movers arrive

**Arrival (Oregon)**
☐ Walk the yard and check fences for gaps before letting the dog off leash
☐ Set up the dog's space first with familiar bed, bowls, and toys
☐ Keep their routine (meal times, walks) as normal as possible
☐ Expect 1–2 weeks of adjustment (clinginess, accidents, poor appetite)
☐ First Oregon vet visit within 2 weeks. Update microchip address. Get the county/city dog license (often required within 30 days of residency).
☐ **Oregon-specific hazards:** foxtails (grass awns) in summer, toxic algae blooms in lakes and rivers, and salmon poisoning disease if dogs eat raw salmon or trout found near streams. Ask your new vet.

## 🚗 OREGON DMV / REGISTRATION CHECKLIST

**Driver's licenses (both of you)**
- [ ] Ohio driver's license
- [ ] Proof of identity, date of birth, and legal presence (passport or certified birth certificate)
- [ ] Social Security number
- [ ] Proof of Oregon address. Bring 2 documents: lease, utility bill, bank statement.
- [ ] REAL ID: decide whether you want one and bring the required documents
- [ ] Expect a vision screening. Knowledge or drive tests are generally waived for valid out-of-state licenses, but verify.
- [ ] Fees (check DMV's current fee schedule)

**Vehicle title and registration (each car)**
- [ ] Ohio title. If there's a lien, follow the lender-to-DMV title process.
- [ ] Current Ohio registration
- [ ] **VIN inspection**, usually done at DMV during the visit (bring the car)
- [ ] Odometer reading (required for most vehicles under 20 years old)
- [ ] Proof of Oregon auto insurance
- [ ] DEQ certificate, if your area requires one
- [ ] Title + registration + plate fees (varies by vehicle MPG and county; some counties add a registration fee)
- [ ] Put the new plates on, and keep the registration card in the car

## 📦 MOVER DELIVERY FOLLOW-UP

**At delivery**
- [ ] Confirm the delivery is inside the Bill of Lading window
- [ ] Check box numbers against the inventory as they come off the truck
- [ ] Inspect furniture before the crew leaves. Write all damage **on the delivery receipt** before signing.
- [ ] Photograph damage, packaging, and inventory tags
- [ ] Confirm reassembly of anything they took apart (if included)
- [ ] Pay the balance by the agreed method and keep the receipt

**After delivery**
- [ ] Open boxes within 1–2 weeks. Hidden damage gets harder to prove over time.
- [ ] File any claim **in writing** with photos, the inventory number, and repair or replacement costs
- [ ] The mover must acknowledge a claim within 30 days and resolve it within 120 days under federal rules
- [ ] If the claim stalls, use the mover's arbitration program or file a complaint with FMCSA's National Consumer Complaint Database

## 🚙 CAR #2 DELIVERY FOLLOW-UP

- [ ] Inspect in daylight, before signing, against your Jul 13 photos
- [ ] Check the odometer against your pickup photo
- [ ] Note any damage **on the carrier's delivery report**. A clean signature makes claims very hard.
- [ ] Photograph all sides and any damage
- [ ] Pay any balance due, which is often cash or certified funds to the driver (confirm in advance)
- [ ] File any damage claim with the carrier promptly. Have the carrier's insurance certificate ready.
- [ ] Reinstall the garage remote and personal items. Add the car to the DMV visit.

## ✅ MISSED ONE-DAY CHECKS (Easy to Forget)

- [ ] **Smoke and CO detectors** at the new place: test them and replace batteries
- [ ] **Change locks** or rekey, and reset garage codes
- [ ] **Find the shutoffs**: water main, breaker panel, gas, sump pump
- [ ] **HVAC filter**: replace it on move-in
- [ ] **Renter's insurance** inventory: upload your photo and serial number records to the new policy
- [ ] **Trash/recycling day**: Oregon recycling rules are stricter than many Ohio cities, so check your hauler's guide
- [ ] **Wildfire and earthquake prep**: sign up for county emergency alerts (most use a service like Everbridge or a local name) and build a go-bag that includes the dog
- [ ] **Air quality**: bookmark AirNow.gov for smoke season (July–September)
- [ ] **Sales tax**: Oregon has none, so expect lower receipts
- [ ] **Gas stations**: Oregon now allows self-serve statewide, but some stations still offer attendants
- [ ] **Spare key** with a trusted neighbor once you know one
- [ ] **Dog ID tag**: order a permanent tag with the new address
- [ ] **Emergency vet**: save the nearest 24-hour vet in both phones
